1: Welcome to Module 6 of the Provider Notices learning path: Google incidents and the maintenance gap.
This is Gate 5 of the provider notices implementation guide, with Chapter 5 of the developer workbook.
Google Cloud's Personalized Service Health lists the incidents relevant to a project or an organization.
So this gate is half collection and half honesty.
In this module you'll read a fictional project's incidents, show that only one kind can ever arrive, and watch the kit refuse an organization-level call that nobody has verified.
The gaps get written down with the I S S O, not papered over.
It takes about forty-five minutes, with a lab on fixtures and a lab in a test project.
The code is illustrative: tested against fixtures, not run against a live project.
2: Why does Google Cloud need a module about a gap?
First, Personalized Service Health's event category has one value, incident, meaning a service outage or degradation.
Planned maintenance isn't in it, and neither are security notices.
Those reach a Google Cloud project by other channels, such as the contacts set in Essential Contacts.

Second, Assured Workloads' supported-products page lists Personalized Service Health under twenty-five regional packages, including U S Data Boundary, but not under fed-ramp Moderate, fed-ramp High, I L 2, I L 4, I L 5, C J I S or I T A R.
A workload in one of those packages has no Personalized Service Health to read at all.
Both gaps share a danger: an empty list looks like good news.
So this gate collects what Google publishes, and writes down, with the I S S O, what can't arrive.

4: The project owner does two things once.
Enable the Service Health A P I on the project, and grant the reader's group the Personalized Service Health Viewer role.
One: cross-check the list with Google's own command, G cloud service health events list, for the project, in the global location.
Two: collect, with the provider set to Google.
For a whole organization, set the settings file's Google scope to organization, and grant the role on the organization.
Otherwise, grant it at the project: the viewer role on the organization, for a project read, is more read scope than the reader needs.
The gate validates when products and locations come from the event's impacts, and closed incidents are closed.
The gate owner is the Google Cloud project owner.
5: Google's Event resource has the one category, a state, a detailed category, relevance, impacts and updates.
Here's what Google leaves to you, and what the kit adds.
With one category, every Google notice is an incident, and the gap is written down in the guide, the chapter and the I S S O's record.
Impacts come as product and location objects; they become the record's services and regions.
An event's description is sometimes empty, so the kit takes the latest update's description.
There's no field that says action is required, and the kit adds no action rule for Google: an open incident that names resources routes by the agency's own routing, in Module 7.
Google's A P I returns a response object and G cloud a bare list, and the kit accepts both.
A closed state closes the record, and the detailed category and relevance are kept as the provider's severity.
The kit has no separate government endpoint for Personalized Service Health; the cloud is global.
6: Two guards make this gate honest.
Google's REST reference documents it, but the G cloud flags for it weren't read.
So the kit's call list marks it unverified, and the live invoker refuses to run it unless you pass allow unverified.
The kit doesn't run a command on a guess.
That's the guide's interim path for an organization.
Every project records that Google's planned maintenance doesn't come through this A P I.
And any workload in an Assured Workloads fed-ramp or I L package records that it has no Personalized Service Health to read; the I S S O decides the compensating channel.
The guide lists the danger plainly: Google maintenance assumed covered, and a maintenance window lands with nobody told.
The guard is the gap itself, in the record, in the digest's provider table and in the I S S O's file.
Until the A P I carries maintenance, it reaches the agency by the contacts it sets.

8: Step four collects the second week, as of November sixteenth.
The same two incidents, and now both are closed.
The Cloud sequel incident ended on November ninth, at thirteen hundred U T C, an hour after the first week's read saw it open.
That's the honest limit of a weekly read: it sees an incident after the fact.
The weekly read is for owning and closing notices, not for detecting incidents, which still reach the desk as calls and alerts first.
Step five groups both weeks by kind.
Four records, and every one an incident.
That's not the fixtures being thin.
It's the A P I: its category has one value.
Maintenance, retirements and security notices never come through this A P I, whatever the project's estate looks like, and that's the gap you write down.

12: First: why does Gate 5 cover incidents only?
The A P I's event category has one value, incident, and planned maintenance isn't in it.
It isn't the kit filtering anything, and it isn't the role.
Second: a workload is in an Assured Workloads fed-ramp Moderate package.

The answer is b. Record the gap with the I S S O. Personalized Service Health isn't among that package's supported products, so the project has nothing to read, and relies on the provider's other channels.
Answer c is the trap this module is about: an empty list doesn't mean no incidents.
